solutions.latex:
The square root is undefined when $x^2-2x-8<0$, so we need

$$x^2-2x-8\ge 0$$

$$(x-4)(x+2)\ge 0$$

$x\in\mathbb{R},\ x\le -2$ or $x\ge 4$. In interval form: $(-\infty,-2]\cup[4,\infty)$.

$\dfrac{x}{3}=\dfrac{y}{x}=\dfrac{192}{y}$, so $x^2=3y$ (1) and $y^2=192x$ (2).

Substituting (2) into (1): $\left(\dfrac{y^2}{192}\right)^2=3y$, so $\dfrac{y^4}{36864}=3y$, giving $y=48$.

Therefore $x=12$ and $y=48$.

Alternatively, $T_4=ar^{3}$: $192=3r^3$, $r^3=64$, $r=4$. Then $x=3\times 4=12$ and $y=12\times 4=48$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: ratio equations (or 192 = 3r^3); 1: substitution / r = 4; 1: x = 12 and y = 48

solutions.latex:
$1+5n=200$, so $5n=199$ and $n=39.8$.

Therefore 200 matchsticks could make the 39th pattern.

Stationary points occur when $y'=0$, i.e. $12x(x-2)^2=0$, so $x=0,2$.

When $x=0$, $y=-9$; when $x=2$, $y=7$. Stationary points are $(0,-9)$ and $(2,7)$.

At $(0,-9)$: $y''=12(-2)(-2)=48>0$, concave up, so a minimum at $(0,-9)$.

At $(2,7)$: $y''=12(0)(4)=0$, possible point of inflexion. Test either side:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 1 & 2 & 3\\ \hline y'' & -12 & 0 & 84\end{array}$$

Concavity changes from down to up, so $(2,7)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.

Other possible points of inflexion when $y''=0$: $12(x-2)(3x-2)=0$, $x=2$ or $x=\tfrac{2}{3}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 0 & \tfrac{2}{3} & 1\\ \hline y'' & 48 & 0 & -12\end{array}$$

Concavity changes, so $\left(\tfrac{2}{3},-\tfrac{67}{27}\right)$ is a point of inflexion.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 4: 1 stationary points found (max 2 marks for points only with no reasons); 1 minimum at (0,-9) with reason; 1 horizontal point of inflexion at (2,7) with table of values; 1 point of inflexion at (2/3, -67/27) with change in concavity

solutions.latex:
Product rule with $u=e^{3x}$, $u'=3e^{3x}$, $v=\cos x-3\sin x$, $v'=-\sin x-3\cos x$:

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)\right]=3e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)+e^{3x}(-\sin x-3\cos x)$$

$$=e^{3x}(3\cos x-9\sin x-\sin x-3\cos x)=-10e^{3x}\sin x$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: product rule applied; 1: simplified to -10 e^{3x} sin x

$$\int e^{3x}\sin x\,dx=-\dfrac{1}{10}e^{3x}(\cos x-3\sin x)+C$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: uses result from (a); 1: correct integral with constant

solutions.latex:
$$\dfrac{dL}{dx}=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}+\dfrac{x-5}{\sqrt{x^2-10x+26}}$$

Stationary point when $\dfrac{dL}{dx}=0$:

$$\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}=\dfrac{5-x}{\sqrt{x^2-10x+26}}\qquad(*)$$

Squaring both sides (note: this introduces an extra solution):

$$\dfrac{x^2}{x^2+4}=\dfrac{(5-x)^2}{x^2-10x+26}$$

$$x^4-10x^3+26x^2=25x^2-10x^3+x^4+100-40x+4x^2$$

$$0=3x^2-40x+100=(3x-10)(x-10)$$

$x=\dfrac{10}{3}$ or $x=10$. But 10 exceeds the construction and does not satisfy $(*)$ (it is the extra solution introduced by squaring). Hence $x=\dfrac{10}{3}$ only.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 0 & \tfrac{10}{3} & 5\\ \hline \dfrac{dL}{dx} & -\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{26}} & 0 & \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{29}}\end{array}$$

$x=\dfrac{10}{3}$ is a local minimum. So $Q$ should be located $\dfrac{10}{3}$ km from $P$ to minimise the length of cable.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: dL/dx; 1: solving to x = 10/3 and rejecting x = 10; 1: test showing minimum and location of Q
1: completing the square; 1: centre and radius

solutions.latex:
$21-(x^2+4x)=21-\left((x+2)^2-4\right)=25-(x+2)^2$.

From $(x+2)^2+(y-1)^2=25$: $y-1=\sqrt{25-(x+2)^2}$, so $y=1+\sqrt{21-4x-x^2}$, the upper semicircle raised by 1.

\exfigure{1281_q27_s1}

Hence the integral is the area of a rectangle plus the area of a semicircle:

$$(3-(-7))\times 1+\dfrac{1}{2}\pi(5)^2=10+\dfrac{25\pi}{2}\ \text{u}^2\approx 49.27\ \text{u}^2\ (\text{2 d.p.})$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: area of rectangle plus area of semicircle; 1: 10 + 25π/2

$v(t)>0$ as $t\ge 0$, so the boat moves in the positive direction.

$$a(t)=v'(t)=-\dfrac{200}{(t+2)^3}$$

Since $t\ge 0$, $(t+2)^3>0$ so $-\dfrac{200}{(t+2)^3}<0$. Velocity is always positively directed and acceleration negatively directed, so acceleration opposes motion.

solutions.latex:
$V=\dfrac{2}{3}(R+x)^2(R-x)$

$$\dfrac{dV}{dx}=\dfrac{2}{3}\left[2(R+x)(R-x)-(R+x)^2\right]$$

Stationary when $\dfrac{dV}{dx}=0$: $0=(R+x)\left[2(R-x)-(R+x)\right]$, so $0=2R-2x-R-x=R-3x$ (as $R\ne -x$; $R,x>0$ as lengths), giving $x=\dfrac{R}{3}$.

$$\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=\dfrac{2}{3}\left[2(-2x)-2(R+x)\right]=-\dfrac{4}{3}(3x+R)$$

When $x=\dfrac{R}{3}$: $\dfrac{d^2V}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{4}{3}(R+R)<0$ as $R>0$, so a local maximum at $x=\dfrac{R}{3}$.

Maximum volume: $V\left(\dfrac{R}{3}\right)=\dfrac{2}{3}\left(R+\dfrac{R}{3}\right)^2\left(R-\dfrac{R}{3}\right)=\dfrac{2}{3}\times\dfrac{16R^2}{9}\times\dfrac{2R}{3}=\dfrac{64}{81}R^3$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: x = R/3; 1: second derivative test; 1: maximum volume 64R^3/81
